q: 301. An outlet is said to be proportional, if its flexibility is
explain: Flexibility is defined as the ratio of the rate of change of discharge of an outlet to the rate of change of discharge of the distributing channel. When this ratio is 1 (unity), the outlet is proportional.

q: 302. The sensitivity of a rigid module is ............
explain: A rigid module maintains a constant discharge regardless of the water level in the distributary or the watercourse; therefore, its sensitivity to changes in the supply level is zero.

q: 303. The flexibility of a hyper-proportional outlet is .......... one.
explain: An outlet is hyper-proportional when its flexibility is greater than unity, meaning the discharge of the outlet changes more rapidly than the discharge of the distributary.

q: 304. For the pipe outlet to be proportional, the outlet is set at .......... the depth below the water surface.
explain: For a pipe outlet to achieve proportionality, the depth of its center below the water surface should be roughly 0.3 times the depth of the channel.

q: 305. The ratio between the depths of water levels over crest on the downstream and upstream of the module, is known as .............
explain: The drowning ratio refers to the ratio of the depth of water on the downstream side of the crest to the depth on the upstream side.

q: 306. Which of the following is a type of non-modular outlet?
explain: A submerged pipe outlet is a non-modular outlet because its discharge depends on the difference in water levels between the distributary and the watercourse.

q: 307. Which of the following is a type of semi-module outlet?
explain: Semi-modules (or flexible modules) like open flume outlets and Kennedy's gauge outlets have discharges that depend only on the water level in the distributary, independent of the watercourse level.

q: 308. The slope of a canal, for a discharge of 300 cumec, should be .............
explain: For large discharges like 300 cumecs, the canal slope is generally flatter; 1 in 6000 is a standard design value for such high-capacity main canals.

q: 309. A diversion head work is constructed to .............
options: raise water level at the head of the canal
regulate the intake of water into the canal
reduce fluctuations in the supply level of the river
explain: Diversion head works serve multiple purposes: raising water level for gravity flow, regulating intake, and controlling silt and river fluctuations.

q: 310. A weir is generally aligned at right angle to the direction of the main river flow because .............
options: less length of weir is required
explain: A perpendicular alignment is the most efficient and economical way to span a river, providing the shortest length and uniform discharge across the crest.

q: 311. A weir fails due to .............
options: rupture of floor due to uplift
rupture of floor due to suction caused by standing wave
scour on the upstream and downstream of the weir
explain: Weirs can fail through subsurface causes (uplift/piping) or surface causes (scouring and impact from hydraulic jumps/standing waves).

q: 312. A solid construction put across the river to raise its water level and divert the water into the canal is known as .............
explain: A weir is a low-height solid obstruction used to raise the water level. While a barrage also does this, the primary definition for a solid construction of this nature is a weir.

q: 313. When the difference in weir crest and downstream river bed is limited into 3 meters, the weir generally used is .............
explain: For moderate drops (up to 3m), a concrete slope (or glacis) weir is preferred to safely guide the water and dissipate energy.

q: 314. In Bligh's creep theory, it is assumed that the percolation water creep .............
options: along the contact of the base profile of the apron with the sub-soil
in a straight path under the floor
in a straight path under the foundation work
explain: Bligh's theory assumes water 'creeps' along the entire length of the contact surface between the structure's base and the soil.

q: 315. In Lane's weighted creep theory, he proposed a weight of .............
options: three for vertical creep and one for horizontal creep
three for horizontal creep and one for vertical creep
two for vertical and two for horizontal creep
explain: Lane suggested that vertical surfaces are three times more effective in resisting piping than horizontal surfaces, thus weightage is 3 for vertical and 1 for horizontal creep.

q: 316. In Bligh's creep theory .............
options: there is no distinction between horizontal and vertical creep
loss of head does not take place in the same proportion as creep length
the uplift pressure distribution is not linear, but follows a sine curve
explain: Unlike Lane's theory, Bligh's theory treats horizontal and vertical creep paths as equally effective in reducing head loss.

q: 317. In a barrage, crest level is kept .............
explain: Barrages typically have a low crest level to allow maximum flood discharge; large gates are then used to control and raise the water level when needed.

q: 318. The loss of head per unit length of creep is called .............
explain: This represents the hydraulic gradient under the structure. Bligh defined the reciprocal of this (length/head) as the Coefficient of Creep (C), but head loss per unit length is the percolation coefficient.

q: 319. According to Khosla's theory, the undermining of the floor starts from the .............
explain: Undermining or piping starts from the downstream (tail) end where the exit gradient is highest and water emerges from the soil.

q: 320. According to Khosla's theory, the exit gradient in the absence of a downstream cut-off is .............
explain: Without a vertical cut-off at the end of the floor, the exit gradient becomes theoretically infinite, leading to immediate piping and failure.

q: 321. A hydraulic jump is formed when .............
options: a sub-critical flow strikes against a super-critical flow
a super-critical flow strikes against a sub-critical flow
the two flows of super-critical velocity meet each other
the two flows of sub-critical velocity meet each other
explain: A hydraulic jump occurs when rapid, super-critical flow transitions to a slower, sub-critical flow state, resulting in energy dissipation.

q: 322. For low navigation dams, the type of gate used is .............
explain: Bear trap gates are often used in navigation because they can be lowered completely to allow vessels to pass over them.

q: 323. The loss of head in the hydraulic jump is given by .............
explain: The energy loss ($H_L$) in a hydraulic jump in a rectangular channel is mathematically expressed as $(D_2 - D_1)^3 / (4 D_1 D_2)$.

q: 324. The crest level in a barrage is kept at a ............. level.
explain: As noted in 317, the physical crest of a barrage is kept low to prevent significant obstruction during high floods.

q: 325. The crest of the under-sluices should be lower than the crest of the head regulator (if silt excluder is provided) by at least .............
explain: The under-sluice pocket is kept lower (usually 1.0 to 1.2m) to create a 'still pond' which helps in settling silt before water enters the canal.

q: 326. For smooth entry, the regulators are aligned at an angle of ............. to the water.
explain: Aligning the head regulator at an angle of 110° to the weir/barrage axis helps in smooth entry of water and effectively reduces silt entry into the canal.

q: 327. The level of a canal diversion head work depends upon .............
explain: The pond level is the most critical factor as it must be high enough to ensure the required Full Supply Level (FSL) in the canal even during low river flow.

q: 328. Rivers on alluvial plains may be .............
explain: Alluvial rivers are dynamic; they can meander (looping), aggrade (deposit sediment), or degrade (scour the bed) depending on silt load and discharge.

q: 329. A river meandering through an alluvial plain has a series of consecutive reversed order connected with short straight sketches, is called .............
explain: A 'crossing' is the relatively short, straight reach of a river between two consecutive reverse bends (meanders).

q: 330. The tortuosity of a meandering river is always ............. one.
explain: Tortuosity is the ratio of the actual curved length along the river channel to the direct axial distance. Since the curve is always longer, the ratio is > 1.

q: 331. The basic factor which controls the process of meandering is .............
explain: Meandering is a complex morphological process influenced by the energy of the water (discharge/slope) and the erodibility of the banks.

q: 332. When river flows in a plain country, its stage is known as ............. stage.
explain: The 'trough' or 'alluvial' stage occurs when the river reaches the plains, characterized by a bed of sand and silt rather than boulders.

q: 333. The width and length of meander as well as width of river, vary approximately with .............
explain: According to regime theories (Lacey/Inglis), meander parameters like width and length are generally proportional to $\sqrt{Q}$ (square root of discharge).

q: 334. The method used for training of rivers is .............
explain: River training involves various structures: Guide banks (flow direction), Levees (flood protection), and Groynes (bank protection/channel narrowing).

q: 335. A river training work is generally required when the river is .............
explain: Meandering rivers are unstable and prone to bank erosion and shifting courses, making training works essential to protect infrastructure.

options: contracts a river channel to improve its depth
silts up the area in the vicinity by creating a slack flow
trains the flow along a certain course
explain: Groynes serve multiple purposes including protecting banks, narrowing the channel for navigation, and encouraging silting in undesired scour zones.

q: 337. A deflecting groyne has a much ............. length than a repelling groyne.
explain: Deflecting groynes are short and only change the local flow direction, whereas repelling groynes are longer and designed to push the main current away.

q: 338. A deflecting groyne in a river is .............
explain: Deflecting groynes are typically inclined downstream (pointing with the flow) to nudge the current away from the bank.

q: 339. A levee on flood .............
options: increases the water surface elevation of the river at flood
decreases the surface slope of the stream above the leveed portion
increases the velocity and scouring action through leveed section
explain: Levees confine floodwaters, which naturally raises the water level, increases velocity due to lack of lateral spread, and changes the energy gradient.

q: 340. A groyne with a curved head is known as .............
explain: A Burma-type groyne is specifically characterized by having a curved or T-shaped head to provide better flow stabilization at the tip.

q: 341. When the bed level of the canal is higher than the highest flood level (H.F.L.) of the drainage, then the cross drainage work is said to be .............
explain: In a simple aqueduct, the canal passes over the drainage with enough clearance that the drainage water never touches the canal bottom.

q: 342. When the drain is over the canal, the structure provided is known as .............
explain: A super-passage is the opposite of an aqueduct; here, the natural drainage (stream) is carried in a trough across and above the canal.

q: 343. When the levels are such that the F.S.L. of the canal is much above the bed level of the drainage trough, so that the canal runs under syphonic action under the trough, the structure provided is known as .............
explain: When the drainage HFL is higher than the canal bed and the canal is forced to dip under the drainage trough, it is a siphon aqueduct.

q: 344. In case of siphon aqueduct, the H.F.L. of the drain is .............
options: much below the bottom of the canal trough
much higher above the canal bed
in level with the canal bed
explain: For syphonic action to occur in the drainage water passing under a canal, the drainage HFL must be higher than the canal bed (or underside of the trough).

q: 345. In a super-passage, the F.S.L. of the canal is .............
options: lower than the underside of the trough carrying drainage water
above the bed level of the drainage trough
in level with the drainage trough
explain: In a super-passage, the canal flow is at atmospheric pressure and its Full Supply Level (FSL) must remain below the bottom of the drainage trough.

q: 346. In a siphon, the underside of the trough carrying drainage water is ............. the F.S.L. of the canal.
explain: In a canal siphon (or siphon aqueduct), the structure is designed such that the canal FSL is actually higher than the bottom of the crossing trough, forcing water to flow under pressure.

q: 347. The bed of a canal is lowered in case of .............
explain: In a canal siphon, the canal bed is depressed or lowered below its normal grade to pass under the drainage/obstruction.

q: 348. The floor of the aqueduct is subjected to uplift pressure due to .............
options: seepage of water from the canal to the drainage
sub-soil water table in the drainage bed
explain: Uplift on the floor can be caused by both the static water table in the surrounding soil and the seepage of water from the canal itself.

q: 349. Canals taken off from ice-fed perennial rivers, are known .............
explain: Perennial canals receive a constant supply of water year-round because their source rivers are fed by melting glaciers/snow.

q: 350. If water table is comparatively high, the irrigation canal becomes useless, due to .............
options: water logging of the cultivated areas
explain: When the water table is high, additional irrigation leads to waterlogging (saturation of the root zone), which prevents aeration and destroys crop productivity.

q: 351. Pick up the incorrect statement from the following. Culturable commanded area is the gross area of an irrigation canal system less .............
explain: Fallow land is technically culturable. CCA is GCA minus non-culturable areas like towns, roads, forests, and barren (alkaline) lands.

q: 352. Optimum depth of kor watering for wheat, is .............
explain: Kor watering is the first watering after sowing. For wheat, the standard optimum depth is approximately 13.5 cm.

q: 353. The optimum depth of kor watering for rice crop, is .............
explain: Rice requires much more water than wheat; the kor watering depth for rice is typically around 19.0 cm.

q: 354. If the optimum depth of kor watering for a crop is 15.12 cm, the outlet factor for the crop for four week period in hectares per cumec, is .............
explain: Outlet factor = $(8.64 \times B) / D$. With $B = 28$ days (4 weeks) and $D = 0.1512$ m, the calculation yields 1600.

q: 355. If V0 is the critical velocity of a channel, its silt transporting power, according to Kennedy, is proportional to .............
explain: Kennedy's theory suggests that the silt-carrying capacity (silt load) of a channel is proportional to $V_0^{2.5}$ or $V_0^{5/2}$.

q: 356. Regime conditions in a channel may occur if .............
options: channel flows uniformly in incoherent alluvium as that transported in suspension
silt grade and silt charge are constant
explain: A 'true regime' channel requires stability in discharge, sediment type, and sediment volume to prevent silting or scouring.

q: 357. Lacey's regime condition is obtained if .............
options: silt grade in the channel is variable
discharge in the channel is variable
silt charge in the channel is variable
channel flows in unlimited, incoherent alluvium of the same character as that transported material
explain: Lacey's theory assumes the channel is flowing in an infinite depth of the same material it is transporting (incoherent alluvium).

q: 358. If average particle size of the silt in millimeters is m, the Lacey's silt factor f is proportional to .............
explain: Lacey's silt factor formula is $f = 1.76 \sqrt{m}$, meaning it is proportional to the square root of the mean particle size.

q: 359. According to Lacey, in regime conditions .............
options: silt is kept in suspension by vertical components of eddies
entire cross-section of the channel is generated at all points by the forces normal to the wetted perimeter
explain: Unlike Kennedy (who only considered vertical eddies from the bed), Lacey stated that eddies are generated from the entire wetted perimeter.

q: 360. The scour depth D of a river during flood, may be calculated from the Lacey's equation .............
explain: The regime scour depth ($R$) for a wide channel is given by $R = 0.47 (Q/f)^{1/3}$.

q: 361. The main cause of silting up a channel, is .............
explain: Silting occurs when the velocity is too low to keep sediment in suspension, caused by poor design, low slopes, or excessive silt entry at the head.

q: 362. F.S.L. of a canal at its head with respect to parent channel is kept .............
explain: The Full Supply Level (FSL) of the taking-off canal is usually kept about 15 cm lower than the parent canal to ensure draw-off even when the parent canal is not at full supply.

q: 363. In gravity canals, F.S.L. is .............
options: generally 4 to 5 meters above the ground level
only a few cm above the ground level
explain: For efficient gravity flow into fields, the canal water level (FSL) should be slightly higher than the surrounding ground level.

q: 364. Side slope generally kept for canals in loam soil are .............
explain: Slopes in cutting can be steeper (1:1) because the natural soil is compact, whereas filling requires flatter slopes (1.5:1) for stability.

q: 365. If d1 is the depth of cutting, d2 is the height of the bank... the horizontal distance n between the bed and bank, is .............
explain: The horizontal distance depends on the slope ($r$) and the height ($d$) of the bank; hence $x = r_2 \times d_2$.

q: 366. Finally formed berms in canals are provided for .............
options: protection of banks erosion by the waves
explain: Berms act as a buffer, reducing wave impact, providing space for sediment to settle (which seals the banks), and widening the bank base for stability.

q: 367. The saturation line is the line up to which banks get saturated after the canal runs for some time. The saturation gradient in ordinary loam soil, is generally .............
explain: In ordinary loam, the phreatic line (seepage line) usually follows a gradient of 4 horizontal to 1 vertical.

q: 368. A counter berm is .............
options: a horizontal benching provided on the inside slope
a horizontal benching provided on the outside slope
a vertical benching provided on the outer edge of the bank
a vertical benching provided on the inner edge of the bank
explain: A counter berm is added to the outside of a canal bank to keep the saturation line well within the body of the bank, preventing leaks.

q: 369. A minimum of 90 cm free board is provided if the discharge in the canal is between .............
explain: Freeboard increases with discharge capacity. For large canals (>60 cumecs), 90 cm (0.9m) is standard.

q: 370. The width of a dowla is generally kept between 30 to 60 cm and its height above the road level should invariably be more than .............
explain: A dowla is a small protective ridge on the edge of the service road. A height of 30 cm is required for safety and to prevent runoff into the canal.

q: 371. A water-logged land is found suitable for cultivation due to .............
options: regular supply of water by capillary action
explain: Waterlogged land is actually unsuitable for most cultivation because the lack of air in the soil 'suffocates' plant roots.

q: 372. The top of the capillary zone .............
options: lies below the water table at every point
lies above the water table at every point
coincides the water table at every point
explain: Capillary action pulls water upward against gravity, so the capillary fringe always sits immediately above the phreatic surface (water table).

q: 373. The measure to remove water logging of land, is .............
options: to increase outflow from the ground water reservoir
explain: Remediation involves both prevention (lining canals to stop seepage) and drainage (pumping or surface drains to lower the water table).

q: 374. If straight sides of a triangular section of a lined canal with circular bottom of radius R, make an angle θ with horizontal, the area of its cross-section, is .............
explain: Based on the geometric properties of a standard triangular canal section with a rounded bottom, the area $A = R^2 (\theta + \cot \theta)$.

q: 375. If the straight sides... make an angle θ with horizontal, the perimeter of the canal is .............
explain: For the same rounded triangular section, the wetted perimeter $P = 2R (\theta + \cot \theta)$.
